patterns.title: AI Adoption vs Compensation — The Productivity Paradox
patterns.question: Do developers who use AI tools daily earn more than those who avoid AI entirely?
patterns.rationale: Counterintuitively, developers who refuse AI tools entirely have the highest average compensation ($110K) while daily AI users earn $101K. This 'paradox' likely reflects that high-earning senior/niche engineers are confident enough not to need AI assistance — a story that challenges the narrative that AI adoption equals productivity gain.

patterns.title: Global Salary Landscape — A 2.5× Gap from US to Europe
patterns.question: What is the average developer compensation across the top 15 countries by respondent count?
patterns.rationale: The US leads at $179K average — 2.5× higher than Germany ($86K) and nearly double the UK ($113K). Ukraine ($105K) outranks Canada ($100K) despite lower GDP per capita, indicating strong remote-work premium effects. A choropleth map exposes these geographic wage disparities at a glance.

patterns.title: Remote Work Premium — Full Remote Pays 67% More Than In-Person
patterns.question: How does work arrangement (remote/hybrid/in-person) affect annual compensation and job satisfaction?
patterns.rationale: Fully remote developers earn $116K on average versus $70K for in-person workers — a 67% premium. Job satisfaction scores (0–10) also skew higher for remote workers, with 'Remote' having the most 10/10 satisfaction scores (1,000 respondents). This dual signal on pay and happiness makes remote work the strongest positive factor in the dataset.

patterns.title: AI Model Market Share — GPT Leads but Claude Holds Strong #2
patterns.question: Which AI models are developers actually using in 2025, and what is the adoption distribution?
patterns.rationale: OpenAI GPT chatbot models dominate with 13,424 users (27% of all respondents), followed by Anthropic Claude Sonnet (7,063) and Google Gemini Flash (5,823). DeepSeek's R-series reasoning models (3,848) already rival Meta Llama (2,941) despite launching in early 2025 — a striking sign of how quickly the market is moving.

patterns.title: AI Job Threat by Experience — Beginners Most Anxious, Veterans Most Confident
patterns.question: Does perceived AI job threat decrease as years of coding experience increases?
patterns.rationale: Among developers with 0–4 years experience, 20% feel AI threatens their job. This drops monotonically to 13–15% in the 5–30 year range and falls to just 7.5% for those with 50+ years. The inverse correlation between experience and AI anxiety is clear and actionable — junior developers need the most reassurance and upskilling support.
